opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it.

The first is simply timing. Around 2012, AlexNet showed that deep learning on GPUs could beat decades of hand-engineered computer vision by a huge margin. By 2013 to 2017 it was clear this wasn't a one-off. Every few months another field, like speech, translation, or game playing, fell to roughly the same recipe. When a field has that kind of momentum, talent goes where the frontier is moving fastest. Young researchers want to work where they can make a big contribution quickly, and AI looked like a land rush.

The second is the barrier to entry and the feedback loop. Deep learning in that period had a very low barrier. You could download PyTorch or TensorFlow, grab a public dataset, change a few lines, train overnight, and get a publishable number. The loop of idea, experiment, result was short, and progress was measured on shared benchmarks. Graphics is different. To do serious work in physical simulation or rendering, you need a lot of background in numerical methods, geometry, linear algebra, and systems programming. Then you write a lot of low-level, performance-critical code, often C++ and CUDA, before you see anything. The ramp is much steeper.

Third, the economics. Big tech companies were pouring money into AI labs and offering very high salaries, because AI connected directly to their core businesses: ads, search, recommendation. Graphics has strong industries too, like film, games, and CAD, but they're smaller and the pay scale wasn't comparable. Students notice that, and so do their advisors.

Fourth, graphics is a fairly mature field. Many of its foundational problems were attacked in the eighties, nineties, and two-thousands, so the low-hanging fruit was largely gone. The remaining problems are hard and specialized. That's intellectually rich, but it's harder to sell to a first-year PhD student than "this new method beats everything."

Personally, though, I don't see it as zero-sum. A lot of what made deep learning take off was tooling. Good frameworks made people productive. Graphics didn't have that same productivity layer, which is part of why I cared about building better programming tools for simulation and rendering. If you lower the barrier, more people can enjoy the field. And looking back, the two areas have converged a lot since then: differentiable rendering, neural representations, physics simulation for robotics and learning. The skills from graphics turned out to be very valuable to AI. So the talent flow made sense at the time, but I think graphics people ended up well positioned for what came next.

r001.rationale: The response explains AI’s momentum, accessibility, and financial incentives, but does not say that many people entering AI had not thought through what they truly liked.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think about this a lot, because I was right in the middle of it. I started doing graphics research around 2013, 2014 as an undergrad at Tsinghua, and I watched a lot of very smart friends make the other choice.

The first thing is just feedback loops. In graphics, if you want to do a new fluid simulation method or a new rendering technique, you might spend six months building infrastructure before you see a single interesting image. In deep learning during that period, you could download a dataset, write a few hundred lines, train overnight, and see a number go up by the next morning. Young people are attracted to fast feedback. That's not a criticism; it's just how motivation works.

The second thing is the sense of an open frontier. Graphics in 2013 was already a very mature field. Siggraph was forty years old. Many of the "big" problems, like photorealistic rendering, had very good solutions, and the remaining problems were hard in a grinding, incremental way. Meanwhile AlexNet had just happened. Every year there was a new result that seemed impossible the year before. When a field feels like it's doubling every year, talented people want to be there, because they feel their individual contribution can actually move the frontier.

The third thing is money and career paths, and we shouldn't pretend that doesn't matter. Around 2015, 2016, companies like Google, Facebook, Baidu were paying very well for machine learning people, and every university was hiring in AI. Graphics had Pixar, had game studios, had a handful of research labs, but the number of positions was much smaller. Students are rational; they look at where their seniors ended up.

And there's a subtler point. AI absorbed graphics' tools and even some of its culture. GPUs were built for rendering, and then CUDA made them the engine of deep learning. So some of the compute expertise that would have gone into graphics went into AI instead, because that was where the hardware was being pushed hardest.

But I'd say the interesting thing is that the two fields didn't really diverge, they converged. The reason I built Taichi was partly this observation: differentiable simulation, neural rendering, physics-based learning, all of these sit exactly on the boundary. A lot of the people who "left" graphics for AI ended up working on problems that look a lot like graphics again. So in hindsight, I don't see 2013 to 2017 as graphics losing talent. I see it as the field being temporarily out of fashion while the ingredients for its comeback were being built next door.

r001.rationale: The response explains AI’s appeal through fast feedback, an open frontier, and stronger career prospects, but does not say that many people entering AI had not thought through what they truly liked.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it was the sense of possibility. Computer graphics already had very impressive results, but many of the problems were quite specialized. To contribute, you often needed to understand a lot of existing techniques, and the improvement might be something that only people in that field could really appreciate.

AI felt different during that period. You could see capabilities improving, and it was easy to imagine those improvements affecting many different industries. For a student choosing a research direction, that’s very attractive: there are interesting technical problems, but also the possibility that your work could have a much broader impact.

And then there’s a feedback loop. Promising results attract investment, investment creates jobs and research opportunities, and those opportunities attract more talented people. I don’t think it means graphics was less intellectually interesting. AI just offered a particularly compelling combination of open problems, momentum, and potential impact.

r001.rationale: The response explains AI’s perceived possibilities, broad impact, and feedback loop, but does not say that many people entering AI had not thought through what they truly liked.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one big reason was that AI offered a very clear sense of momentum. You could take a problem that people had worked on for years, apply deep learning, and suddenly get a much better result. For a young researcher, that’s very exciting: you can see both the opportunity to contribute and the potential impact of your work.

Computer graphics was already a relatively mature field. There were still many interesting problems, but making progress often required a lot of specialized knowledge and careful engineering. The progress could feel more incremental.

AI also seemed applicable to almost everything—vision, language, robotics—so it attracted people from many different backgrounds. And once companies started investing heavily, there were more resources and career opportunities. That created a feedback loop: exciting results attracted talent, and more talent produced more exciting results.

r001.rationale: The response explains AI’s momentum, broad applicability, and career opportunities, but does not say that many entrants had not thought through what they truly liked.
